name: The divided line: Reason versus Understanding
plain_explanation: Plato distinguishes two kinds of intellectual activity: 'understanding,' used in mathematics, which relies on unquestioned starting assumptions (like 'let ABC be a triangle'), and 'reason,' the higher kind, which grasps the Ideas themselves directly through dialectic, without needing any hypotheses.
precise_definition: Plato's division of the intellect (as opposed to sense-perception) into 'understanding' (dianoia), which reasons hypothetically from unproved assumptions as in geometry, and 'reason' (nous), which proceeds dialectically to unconditioned knowledge of the Ideas, especially the Idea of the Good.
why_it_mattered: It explains why Plato regards mathematics, for all its rigor, as inferior to dialectic: mathematics can never tell us what truly is, only what would be true if its hypotheses held.
historical_origin: Developed as part of the sixth and seventh books of the Republic's account of philosophical education.
examples: Geometry says 'let ABC be a rectilinear triangle,' but no drawn figure is truly rectilinear, so geometry only yields hypothetical truth about an unseen, super-sensible triangle.
objections: Russell notes an unresolved difficulty Plato seems to have missed: if God made only one bed, he must, on the same logic, have made many straight lines (for a triangle needs three), which threatens to demote geometry itself to the status of mere appearance.
